chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Johnny Dunn and the cup mute origin story
summary: Briggs says Johnny Dunn imitated Keppard but told him he discovered the effect himself with a cup; they worked together at the Sporting Club in Monte Carlo.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Right. He was a freak player then, really?
He was really a freak player. A technical freak player.
Right. He knew what he was doing.
He knew what he was doing. He was a -- you heard in later years, you heard of Johnny Dunn?
Briggs
Sure.
Johnny Dunn was an imitation of what Freddie Keppard was doing.
Oh, was he?
Oh yes, sure.
So Johnny Dunn got that off of Freddie Keppard then?
He got that himself -- he probably did. The idea, or something happened. Johnny told me himself, because for a short time we worked together at the Sportin' in Monte Carlo.

Johnny told me when he said, -- it would happen -- "I was messing around with my horn in my room, and I had a cup on the table, and I took the cup and blew, and I took another one and blew, used a cup, you know, in the bell," and he said, "My God," and I really realized I got something," see.
He said, "That's how I found it." But I'd heard that Freddie Keppard
Briggs
did the same thing with a tin can. So Johnny Dunn told you this story, that he figured it out for himself.
Yes, he said, for himself. But really Freddie Keppard is the one --
Yes, because Keppard you know, Keppard was in the Wintergarden in New York in 1915, or something like that.
Yes. He was.
He was.
I was too young then. I didn't see him.
